covers.quote: Like other punctuation marks, question marks stay with the text they refer to. Usually, this is immediately after the last letter of the last word of the sentence.
Brackets and quotation marks change the position of question marks
For brackets and quotation marks, place the question mark:
before a closing bracket or quotation mark if the question is part of the text in the brackets or quotation marks
after the closing bracket or quotation mark if the question is part of the surrounding text.
Question marks can express doubt and uncertainty about dates or other specific details.

rules.quote: Question marks usually go after the last letter in a sentence
rules.violation_condition: A question mark does not immediately follow the text it punctuates, or is on the wrong side of a closing bracket or quotation mark for the scope of the question.
when: Applies to question marks punctuating questions.
If the question belongs to the text inside brackets or quotation marks, the question mark goes before the closing delimiter.
If the question belongs to the surrounding text, the question mark goes after the closing delimiter.
Question marks inserted to express uncertainty about dates or other details are outside this sentence-ending placement check.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates the default placement and delimiter-dependent cases; G-3 excludes optional uncertainty markers; G-4 absorbs the explanatory wording.

covers.quote: Users expect direct questions and requests to end with a question mark.
Direct questions end with a question mark.
Some sentences don’t start with one of the words such as ‘who’, ‘could’ and ‘does’ but still end with a question mark.
Sometimes questions are tagged on to the end of another clause.
Requests are often framed as questions.
Rhetorical questions end in a question mark or exclamation mark
Depending on the context, a rhetorical question can end in a question mark or an exclamation mark.

rules.quote: Direct questions and requests end in a question mark
rules.violation_condition: A direct question or request framed as a question lacks a closing question mark, unless it is a rhetorical question ending with an exclamation mark.
when: Includes questions that do not begin with a conventional interrogative or auxiliary word.
Includes questions tagged onto another clause.
Applies to requests framed as questions, not to commands or instructions.
A rhetorical question may end with an exclamation mark instead.
rules.why: G-2 keeps question forms and the rhetorical-question exception together; G-3 treats the permitted exclamation mark as an exception; G-4 consolidates restatements.

covers.quote: Indirect questions don’t end with question marks, even if they include a word such as ‘who’ or ‘does’.
Indirect questions are often used in headings.
Instructions and commands aren’t framed as questions.
They don’t start with words such as ‘what’, ‘are’ or ‘does’,and don’t end with a question mark.

rules.quote: Indirect questions and commands don’t use a question mark
rules.violation_condition: An indirect question, command or instruction is punctuated with a closing question mark.
when: An indirect question remains covered even if it contains a word such as ‘who’ or ‘does’.
Also applies to indirect questions used as headings.
Requests actually framed as direct questions are not commands for this check.
rules.why: G-2 combines the stated cases of inappropriate question-mark endings; G-4 absorbs the body restatements without creating a separate rule about opening words.

covers.quote: To turn indirect questions into direct questions you can:
introduce a word such as ‘can’ or ‘why’ – but make sure there is a subject.

rules.quote: make sure there is a subject.
rules.specification: The subject requirement is explicitly attached to the suggested conversion method. The page does not establish whether it should extend to other direct questions or question fragments, and conversion history may not be recoverable from the resulting text.
rules.violation_condition: A direct question formed by introducing a word into an indirect question lacks a grammatical subject.
when: An indirect question is being turned into a direct question by introducing a word such as ‘can’ or ‘why’.
rules.why: The optional conversion method is not itself a rule under G-3, but its explicit subject requirement describes a text property; the uncertain scope is deferred rather than generalised.
